essentials: China is building a **national sustainability reporting system**, the Corporate Sustainability Disclosure Standards (CSDS), to be in place by **2030**.
The **Basic Standard** (2024), its application guidelines and the **Climate Standard** (2025) are published. They are **trial and voluntary** for now.
Separately, the **stock exchanges** already require reports from large listed companies, first due by 30 April 2026.
The standards follow the **ISSB** model and add the company's **impacts**, which brings them close to the EU's double materiality.

sections.title: Why it matters outside China
text: Chinese suppliers are increasingly asked for sustainability data by foreign customers, each with their own format. A national standard gives them one framework to prepare data in, and it tells buyers what information will become available without asking. For foreign groups, subsidiaries in China may come under the rules as they move from voluntary to mandatory.

after: The Ministry of Finance leads the work together with eight other authorities, among them the central bank, the securities regulator and the environment ministry.

sections.title: Voluntary now, mandatory in steps
text: The ministry has described the path as moving from listed to unlisted companies, from large to small and medium-sized, from qualitative to quantitative information and from voluntary to mandatory disclosure. No general start date for mandatory application of the national standards has been set; regulators decide by sector and company type.

sections.title: The stock-exchange guidelines
points: The exchanges in Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing issued sustainability reporting guidelines in 2024.
Reporting is **mandatory** for constituents of the main indices (SSE 180, STAR 50, SZSE 100, ChiNext) and for companies listed both in mainland China and abroad.
First reports, for financial year 2025, were due by **30 April 2026**.
The guidelines use **double materiality**: financial effects on the company and the company's effects on the economy, society and the environment.

mistakes.wrong: All companies in China must already report under the CSDS.
mistakes.right: The national standards are voluntary for now. Only the exchange guidelines are mandatory, for certain listed companies.

mistakes.wrong: The Chinese standards are a copy of the ISSB.
mistakes.right: They build on it but also require information on the company's impacts.

mistakes.wrong: This has no relevance for foreign buyers.
mistakes.right: It determines what data suppliers will have and in which format.

practice: **Identify listed suppliers** that already publish exchange reports and use those reports first.
**Align your data requests** with the Basic and Climate Standards where possible, so suppliers prepare data once.
**Watch announcements** on mandatory application by sector.

quiz.q: What is the status of China's national sustainability disclosure standards in 2026?
options: Published on a trial, voluntary basis
quiz.why: The Basic and Climate Standards are trial standards for voluntary use, with a path towards mandatory application.

quiz.q: By when is the unified national system to be in place?
Which companies must already publish sustainability reports under the exchange guidelines?
options: Constituents of the main indices and dual-listed companies
quiz.why: The mandatory group covers large listed companies in the main indices and those listed in mainland China and abroad.

quiz.q: Which international model do the Chinese standards build on?
quiz.why: Structure and climate content follow IFRS S1 and S2, with impact information added.
